meta.title: Memory across coding agents, for solo developers
meta.description: Share project memory across coding agents and machines connected to one server. Plain Markdown, with no model-provider key for default memory features.

hero.title: Stop re-explaining your project
hero.lede: Save decisions, failed approaches and unfinished work for your next agent session. A PC and notebook can share that memory when both reach the same server. Default memory features need no model-provider API key.

handoff.title: Switch agents in the middle of a task
handoff.lede: Hit a rate limit in Claude Code at 4 PM. Open Codex in the same directory and keep going.
handoff.figureAlt: Diagram: a Claude Code session ends and passes a handoff baton through ai-memory to a Codex session. The handoff holds a summary, next steps and open questions. A second terminal that reaches for the same baton is locked out because it was claimed once.
handoff.figureCaption: The handoff is matched by project directory, so the next agent only has to start in the same checkout.

items.title: Typed
items.text: A handoff carries a session summary, the next steps and the open questions. The next agent gets it at session start, before you type anything.

items.title: Even when nothing ended
items.text: A quota limit or a crash writes no handoff. The next session is pointed at that unfinished work by name, and can read its observations.

items.title: Claimed exactly once
items.text: The first eligible session claims the handoff. A second request cannot claim the same one. This prevents duplicate delivery of that handoff, not two agents independently choosing similar work.

items.title: Automatic, with a manual override
items.text: Every session end writes one. Say "save context for the next session" to write your own, and yours outranks the automatic one.

handoff.exceptions: Two agents, Grok Build CLI and Zero, ignore what hooks print at session start. Ask them to accept the handoff and they fetch it over MCP. The integrations page lists every agent and what each one supports.

phrases.title: What you say day to day
phrases.lede: Most days you say nothing. Hooks capture the session, and the session end turns it into wiki pages. When you do want something, plain English is the interface.

items.does: Reads the pending handoff: summary, next steps, open questions.
Searches the wiki with full text, entities, links and vectors fused into one ranking.

items.say: “Catch me up. I have been away.”
items.does: Builds a digest that gets longer the longer you were gone. It is prose with an LLM configured, structured data without one.
Writes a durable, git-versioned page. Pin it and it never decays.
Writes the page with an expiry date. The forget sweep deletes it after that.
Records feedback for retention and lint. It does not change search ranking or directly delete the page.

phrases.more: The usage guide on GitHub has the full list of phrases and the MCP tool behind each one.

launcher.title: One launcher, and a way in for old projects

run.title: Start your agent with ai-memory run
points: The first launch installs that agent’s hooks and MCP entry if they are missing. It does this once per agent.
Switching agents resumes the same workstream, with the visible history on top of the summary handoff.
ai-memory continue finds your most recent checkout from any directory and resumes there.
It covers {n} agents today. Launching an agent directly keeps working, and hooks alone already carry the handoff.
run.commentSwitch: Quit Claude Code, then continue the same workstream in Codex.
run.commentContinue: From any directory: put me back where I was.

adopt.title: Adopt a project you already have
adopt.text: The first session in an empty project imports your local agent history once, capped at the newest 25 sessions. You can also run it by hand.

backfill.comment: See what would be imported, then import it
backfill.note: Opt out of the automatic first-run import with AI_MEMORY_BACKFILL_ON_START=false.

bootstrap.codeTitle: seed the wiki from the repository
bootstrap.comment: Needs an LLM provider on the server
bootstrap.note: Bootstrap reads the git log, the README, docs/ and your rule files. The project measured a run at well under $0.20 with Kimi 2.6 through OpenRouter. It can write pages that sound right and are wrong, so read the dry run first.

machines.title: The same memory on your PC and your notebook
machines.lede: Run one server and point your machines at it. By default, project identity comes from the Git remote; folders without a valid remote use their directory name. Marker files can override this, so check the resolved project when connecting a second machine.
machines.figureAlt: Diagram: a PC and a notebook both connect to one ai-memory server. The notebook is offline, so its events wait in a local spool and drain to the server later. There is only one server.
points: Put the server on a homelab box, or on whichever machine stays on. It is one binary or one container.
When the notebook is offline, hook events go to a local spool and drain when the server is reachable again. Each entry has an idempotency key, so nothing is stored twice.
ai-memory status shows how many events are pending and how old the oldest is.
Remote access needs a bearer token and TLS, even within your LAN. Configure both before connecting another machine.
machines.codeTitle: point a machine at the server
machines.comment: On the PC and on the notebook

callout.title: One server, no replication
callout.text: Machines share memory because they reach the same server. Two servers do not sync with each other, and pointing two servers at one synced data folder is unsupported because the wiki does not survive it. The advanced setup page covers the homelab install, TLS and backups.

defaults.title: Local memory and readable files
defaults.lede: The default install costs nothing to run and stores everything as markdown in a git repository.

items.title: Zero LLM calls
items.text: Capture, session summaries, handoffs and search all run without a model. Summaries are rule based until you add a provider.

items.title: Embeddings run in the binary
items.text: A small local model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, about 87 MB) downloads once in the background. Vector search turns on at the next restart. It needs no key and no GPU.

items.title: Loopback only
items.text: The default server listens on 127.0.0.1:49374 with no account and no telemetry. Nothing else on the network can reach it.

defaults.figureAlt: Diagram: a wiki folder of plain markdown files at the centre, with spokes to grep, Obsidian, a text editor and rsync, and a git history underneath.
defaults.figureCaption: Edit a page in Obsidian or vim and a file watcher updates the search index.

files.title: Take the files anywhere
files.text: You can read and edit the Markdown pages. Reindex rebuilds their search index, but sessions, handoffs and accounts also need the database. Use ai-memory backup; a git push of the wiki alone is not a full backup.
files.codeTitle: the wiki is a git repo
files.commentCopy: Copy the wiki out of the container and open it in Obsidian

web.title: A browser for your memory
web.text: One flag opens the browser dashboard with projects, activity, saved pages, search and inboxes. Wiki pages remain read-only here; authorized users can send or edit pending messages.
web.shotAlt: Screenshot of the 3.3.0 project overview with tabs for agents, token usage, sessions and knowledge, plus capture counts and pending mail.
web.shotCaption: The project dashboard separates captured sessions from compiled pages. Open a tab to inspect activity, response usage or saved knowledge.

callout.title: Claude Code’s built-in memory may be enough
callout.stay: If you work alone, on one machine, and only use Claude Code, stay with its built-in memory. It is already on and has no server to run.
callout.stops: It stops being enough when you:
reasons: add a second agent, because that memory belongs to Claude Code alone
add a second machine, because it lives on one laptop
want to search months of sessions, including what the tools did
callout.compare: The comparison page covers this and the other memory tools, including where they are ahead.

faq.q: Do I need an API key or an LLM to use ai-memory?
faq.a: No. Capture, session summaries, handoffs and search work with zero LLM calls. Embeddings for vector search run in-process with a local model. An LLM provider is optional and adds richer consolidation, bootstrap and reranking.

faq.q: Do I have to use ai-memory from the first day of a project?
faq.a: No. Add it at any point. The first session in a project with no memory yet imports the agent sessions already on your machine, from every supported agent, up to the newest 25. It runs once, in the background, with no LLM. ai-memory bootstrap can also build pages from the git log, the README and your docs, and that one needs an LLM.

faq.q: Can I use the same memory on a PC and a notebook?
faq.a: Yes. Run one ai-memory server on a homelab box or on one of the machines and point both at it. There is no replication between servers. If the notebook is offline, hook events spool locally and drain when the server is reachable again.

faq.q: Is Claude Code’s built-in memory enough?
faq.a: For one developer on one machine who only uses Claude Code, it may be. It stops being enough when you add a second agent, a second machine or a second person.
Reindex rebuilds pages, links and full-text search from Markdown. It cannot recover database-only sessions, observations, handoffs, users, keys or audit records.
